prompt: Which of these is how Go writes a loop that repeats while `n > 1`?
hint: Go has one keyword for loops.

choices.text: `while n > 1 { … }`
choices.why: `while` is not one of Go's keywords; section 02 shows the syntax error it causes.

choices.text: `do { … } while n > 1`
choices.why: Go has no `do … while` either; every loop is a `for`.
Right. A `for` with only a condition is Go's `while`.

choices.text: `for range n > 1 { … }`, with `range` before the condition
choices.why: `range` needs something to walk, and a condition is a `bool`: `cannot range over n > 1 (untyped bool value)`.

prompt: `for i := 0; i < 3; i++ { … }` runs its body three times. How many times is the condition `i < 3` tested?
hint: Follow the figure: the test that ends the loop is a test too.

prompt: A `fmt.Println(i)` placed right after `for i := 0; i < 3; i++ { … }` does what?
hint: Where was `i` declared?

choices.text: Prints 3, the value that ended the loop
choices.why: That would be true if `i` outlived the loop; declared in the first clause, it does not.

choices.text: Prints 2, the last value the body saw
choices.why: The line does not compile, so it prints nothing at all.

choices.text: It does not compile: `undefined: i`, because `i` belongs only to the loop
choices.why: Right. The variable of the first clause belongs to the `for` statement.

choices.text: Prints 0, since `i` is reset when the loop ends
choices.why: Nothing resets it; it is simply out of scope.

prompt: A module's `go.mod` says `go 1.21`. Which of these loops compile in it? Choose all that apply.
hint: Section 02 changed the `go` line and ran again.

choices.why: Yes. The three-clause loop has always been Go.

choices.text: `for i := range 3 { … }`
choices.why: No: `cannot range over 3 (untyped int constant): requires go1.22 or later`.
Yes. A condition alone is as old as the three clauses.

choices.text: `for range 2 { … }`
choices.why: No. Ranging over an integer, with or without a variable, arrived in Go 1.22.

prompt: A file fails with `syntax error: unexpected name n at end of statement` on the line `while n > 1 {`, and with a second error on line 10 about a statement outside the function body. What should be fixed?
hint: Which error caused the other?

choices.text: Line 10 first, because the last error in the list is the real one
choices.why: It is the other way round: the parser lost track of the braces because of the first error.

choices.text: `while` becomes `for`; the line 10 error then goes with it
choices.why: Right. Fix the first error and run again; the second was the parser stumbling over the same mistake.

choices.text: Rename `n`, since the message says it is unexpected
choices.why: `n` is unexpected only because `while` before it is read as a name; any name there fails the same way.

choices.text: Write `while (n > 1) {`, with parentheses, as in C
choices.why: Parentheses do not make `while` a keyword; Go has none by that name.

prompt: `for i := ___ 5 { … }` runs its body five times, with `i` going from 0 to 4.
hint: The word that also walks slices, maps and strings.

prompt: What does `for x := range []string{"a", "b"} { fmt.Println(x) }` print?
hint: One variable, over a slice.

choices.text: `a` and then `b`
choices.why: That is Python's `for x in xs`. In Go one variable gets the index.

choices.text: `0` and then `1`
choices.why: Right. With one variable, `range` over a slice gives the indices, whatever the variable is called.

choices.text: `0 a` and then `1 b`
choices.why: Both would need two variables, `for i, x := range …`.

choices.text: Nothing, because one variable is refused and `_` is required
choices.why: One variable is allowed; `_` is how you skip the index when you want the elements.

prompt: `team` holds `{Ana 10}` and `{Bia 7}`. After `for _, p := range team { p.Score += 5 }`, what does `fmt.Println(team)` print?
hint: What is `p` on each pass?

choices.why: That needs writing through the index, `team[i].Score`; `p` was a copy.

choices.text: `[{Ana 10} {Bia 7}]`, the scores unchanged
choices.why: Right. Each `p` was a copy of an element, changed and thrown away.

choices.text: `[{Ana 10} {Bia 12}]`, since only the last copy is written back
choices.why: No copy is ever written back, the last one included.

choices.text: Nothing, because `go vet` refuses a loop that changes its copy
choices.why: `go vet` exited 0 on exactly this loop, and `go run` does not run vet anyway.

prompt: Which loop really adds 5 to every player's `Score` in the slice `team`?
hint: The loop has to write to the slice, not to a copy.

choices.text: `for _, p := range team { p.Score += 5 }`
choices.why: `p` is a copy of each element, so the slice is untouched.

choices.text: `for p := range team { p.Score += 5 }`
choices.why: With one variable `p` is the index, an `int`: `p.Score undefined (type int has no field or method Score)`.

choices.text: `for i := range team { team[i].Score += 5 }`
choices.why: Right. `team[i]` is the element in the slice itself.

choices.text: `for i, p := range team { p.Score = team[i].Score + 5 }`
choices.why: It reads the right value and still writes it into the copy `p`.

prompt: `nums := []int{1}`, then `for _, n := range nums { nums = append(nums, n+1) }`. What does `fmt.Println(nums)` print?
hint: When does `range` decide how many passes there will be?

choices.text: No output: the loop keeps finding the element it just appended, and runs forever
choices.why: That is what a three-clause loop testing `len(nums)` would do; `range` read the length once.

choices.text: `[1 2]`: one pass, since `nums` held one element when the loop began, and one append
choices.why: Right. The slice had one element when the loop started, so there was one pass.

choices.text: `[1]`, because an `append` inside `range` is discarded
choices.why: The append is kept, since its result is assigned back to `nums`; it just adds no passes.

choices.text: A panic, as changing a slice while ranging over it is forbidden
choices.why: It is allowed; section 03 appended inside a `range` and printed `[1 2 3 10 20 30]`.

prompt: Which of these are true of `for i, v := range s`, where `s` is a slice? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two are about copies and counts; two are about variables.

choices.text: `v` is a copy of `s[i]`
choices.why: Yes. `range` assigns the element to `v`, and assignment copies.

choices.text: Assigning to `v` changes `s[i]`
choices.why: No. The team kept its old scores for exactly this reason.

choices.text: The number of passes is fixed when the loop starts
choices.why: Yes. `range` reads the slice once, before the first pass.

choices.text: Since Go 1.22, `i` and `v` are one pair reused on every pass
choices.why: It is the reverse: since 1.22 each pass gets its own `i` and `v`.

prompt: What values does `i` take in `for i := range "café"`?
hint: The `é` takes two bytes.

choices.why: Those are the byte indices a three-clause loop over `len(s)` walks; `range` stops once per rune.

choices.text: 1, 2, 3 and 4, one per character
choices.why: Offsets start at 0, and they count bytes, not characters.

choices.text: 0, 1, 2 and 3: one offset per rune, where each begins
choices.why: Right. Four runes, each at the byte offset where it starts; the `é` starts at 3.

choices.text: 0, 1, 2 and 5, the offset just past the `é`
choices.why: The offset is where a rune starts, not where it ends.

prompt: `range` meets the byte `\xff`, which begins no UTF-8 character. What does it do?
hint: Section 04 printed one line for it.

choices.text: It panics with an invalid UTF-8 error
choices.why: Nothing failed: the loop carried on to the `!`.

choices.text: It gives the rune U+FFFD and moves on by one byte
choices.why: Right. The replacement character, `utf8.RuneError`, and the next pass starts at the next byte.

choices.text: It skips the byte without a pass
choices.why: There was a pass for it, at offset 5, printing `U+FFFD`.

choices.text: It gives the byte itself, 255, as the rune
choices.why: The rune was U+FFFD, not U+00FF; `range` decodes, and a byte that decodes to nothing gets the replacement.

prompt: `len("señor")` is 6, because `ñ` takes two bytes. How many passes does `for range "señor"` make?
hint: One pass per rune.

prompt: A loop over a map deletes every entry whose value is 0, inside the same `range`. What happens?
hint: Section 04 did exactly this with `stock`.

choices.text: It works: every such entry is gone, whatever order the walk took
choices.why: Right. Deleting while walking a map is allowed, and `stock` kept only `apples` and `plums`.

choices.text: A compile error: `delete` cannot appear inside a `range` over the same map
choices.why: The compiler does not look for that, and the program in section 04 ran.

choices.text: A fatal error about the map being changed during iteration
choices.why: That kind of failure belongs to two goroutines sharing a map, the `go-concurrency` course's subject; one loop is fine.

choices.text: Some entries survive, since the walk skips whatever follows a deletion
choices.why: Every zero was removed; a deletion hides only the entry deleted.

prompt: A report must list a map's entries in the same order every time it runs. Which loop gives that?
hint: Only one of them sorts anything.

choices.text: `for k, v := range m`
choices.why: Lesson 14 ran the same walk twice and got two orders.

choices.text: `for k := range maps.Keys(m)`
choices.why: `maps.Keys` hands out keys in the map's own order, which is random.

choices.text: `for k, v := range m`, run twice so the order settles
choices.why: The order never settles; it is chosen again on every walk.

choices.text: `for _, k := range slices.Sorted(maps.Keys(m))`
choices.why: Right. The keys are sorted into a slice, and a slice is walked in index order.

prompt: `maps.Values(m)` returns an ___: a function that `range` calls to receive the values one at a time.
hint: Its type is `iter.Seq[V]`.

prompt: Match what is ranged over to what the first variable holds.
hint: The table at the end of section 04.

pairs.right: The byte offset where a rune starts

right_distractors: The number of characters seen so far

prompt: Put the steps of `for i := 0; i < 2; i++ { body }` in the order they happen, from the start to the end of the loop.
hint: The condition is tested before every pass, and once more at the end.
items: `i < 2` is false, and the loop ends

prompt: `for i, r := range s` printed the offsets 0, 1, 3 and 4. What do you know about the rune at offset 1?
hint: The gap between two offsets is the size of the rune between them.

choices.text: It is a broken byte, replaced by U+FFFD
choices.why: After a broken byte `range` moves on by one byte, so the next offset would be 2.

choices.text: No conclusion: offsets can jump for any rune
choices.why: They jump by exactly the size of the rune, which is what makes the gap readable.

choices.text: It took two bytes, so it is not ASCII
choices.why: Right. The next rune starts at 3, two bytes on, and every ASCII character is one byte.

choices.text: The loop skipped the rune at offset 2
choices.why: No rune starts at 2; that byte is the second half of the rune at 1.
